title: De Bello Gallico - Book I, Opening
author: Gaius Julius Caesar
description: Caesar's account of the Gallic Wars, written in third person. This opening describes the geography and peoples of Gaul.

sections.latin: Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres, quarum unam incolunt Belgae, aliam Aquitani, tertiam qui ipsorum lingua Celtae, nostra Galli appellantur.
sections.translation: All Gaul is divided into three parts, one of which the Belgae inhabit, another the Aquitani, and a third those who in their own language are called Celts, in ours Gauls.

vocabulary.form: perf pass part nom sg f

grammaticalNotes: Gallia est divisa: periphrastic perfect passive (est + perfect participle)
quarum: genitive of the whole (partitive genitive)
qui...appellantur: relative clause with implied antecedent

sections.latin: Hi omnes lingua, institutis, legibus inter se differunt.
sections.translation: All these differ among themselves in language, customs, and laws.
grammaticalNotes: lingua, institutis, legibus: ablatives of respect/specification
inter se: reflexive with preposition meaning 'among themselves'

sections.latin: Gallos ab Aquitanis Garumna flumen, a Belgis Matrona et Sequana dividit.
sections.translation: The Garonne river separates the Gauls from the Aquitani, the Marne and Seine from the Belgae.
grammaticalNotes: ab Aquitanis, a Belgis: ablative of separation with preposition
Double subject (Matrona et Sequana) with singular verb (dividit) - common in Latin

sections.latin: Horum omnium fortissimi sunt Belgae, propterea quod a cultu atque humanitate provinciae longissime absunt.
sections.translation: Of all these, the Belgae are the bravest, because they are furthest from the civilization and refinement of the Province.
grammaticalNotes: Horum omnium: partitive genitive with superlative
a cultu: ablative of separation with absum

historicalContext: Caesar wrote the Commentarii de Bello Gallico during his campaigns in Gaul (58-50 BCE). The work served both as a military report to the Senate and as political propaganda to enhance his reputation in Rome.
literaryFeatures: Third-person narrative (Caesar refers to himself as 'Caesar')
Ethnographic digressions on Gallic and Germanic customs
Careful attention to geography and logistics
